body.heading: The instant reply trap
paragraphs: Messages arrive with built-in urgency, and a reply typed in the first flash of irritation or anxiety often says more than we meant. The sender cannot see your face, so words carry everything — including the mood you were in for ten seconds.
A single slow breath is a surprisingly effective gap. It is long enough for the first reaction to peak and start fading, and short enough that nobody notices the pause.

body.heading: A tiny routine for tricky messages
paragraphs: Read the message. Breathe in slowly, and out even more slowly. Read it once more, as if it were written by someone having a hard day. Then reply to the message itself, not to your first interpretation of it.
And some messages deserve more than a breath — they deserve an hour, or a conversation in person instead. “Let me think about that and come back to you” is a complete and respectable reply.

takeaway: One breath before you type: the smallest pause that changes replies.
